meta.title: Ride Hailing
meta.summary: Match riders to nearby drivers in real time (Uber / Lyft style), with live location streaming and payment at trip end.

functional: Drivers stream their location while online
Riders request a ride and are matched to a nearby available driver
Driver accepts or declines an offer; rider sees the assigned driver and ETA
Fare is computed and charged when the trip ends
nonFunctional: A driver can never be assigned to two trips at once
Location updates every ~4 s per active driver
Each city keeps working if one zone fails

scale.label: Location writes
scale.value: ~250k/s at peak (1M drivers / 4 s), ~100k/s averaged over the day

scale.label: Rider tracking
scale.value: about half of all updates come from drivers on a trip and are pushed to a rider

slos.name: Time to match
slos.sli: Ride requests with a driver assigned within the threshold, divided by all requests, measured by the matching service

slos.name: Trip API availability
slos.sli: Trip requests that succeed divided by all trip requests, at the load balancer

slos.name: Driver position freshness
slos.sli: Driver positions in the index newer than the threshold, divided by all online drivers

slos.name: Charged once
slos.sli: Completed trips charged exactly once, divided by completed trips, from nightly reconciliation

slos.name: One trip per driver
slos.sli: Drivers with at most one active trip, divided by drivers on a trip, from refused second assignments and an audit query; good means no driver ever has two

alerts.when: Unmatched requests above 10% for 5 minutes while drivers are available nearby
alerts.why: Riders are waiting and drivers are idle, which means matching is broken, not that supply is low.

alerts.when: Trip API errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Riders cannot request or complete trips.

alerts.when: Trip API errors burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow leak that would use up the month's budget in ten days.

alerts.when: Any trip charged more than once, found by reconciliation
alerts.why: It is money, and trust is hard to win back. Stop and fix.

alerts.when: More than 5% of online drivers have a position older than 20 seconds
alerts.why: Matching starts offering drivers who have already moved.

alerts.when: WebSocket disconnects above 3 times the normal rate for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Usually a gateway deploy or a network problem. Drivers drop out of the pool.

alerts.when: Any second assignment refused by the one-active-trip index, or the audit finds a driver on two trips
alerts.why: A refused assignment means the busy flags failed (often a Redis failover); a driver on two trips means the guard failed too.

alerts.when: Trip Tracker iterator age above 30 seconds for 5 minutes
alerts.why: Riders see the car frozen on the map, and fares wait for traces.

alerts.when: More than 1% of completed trips still payment pending after 1 hour
alerts.why: The provider is failing or the retry job is stuck; unpaid trips are revenue at risk.

alerts.when: Maps provider errors above 2% or p99 above 1 s for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Matching cannot rank by road ETA; fall back to straight-line distance.

signals.name: Unmatched requests by reason
signals.why: Separates no drivers nearby from lock contention and map provider failures.

signals.name: Open connections per node
signals.why: A node near its limit drops connections and causes a reconnect storm.

signals.name: Position updates per second against expected
signals.why: A sudden drop usually means an app or gateway problem, not drivers going offline.

signals.name: Requests against matches per city
signals.why: The business view: match rate per city shows supply problems before riders complain.

signals.name: Stream lag
signals.why: How far behind real time the rider's map and the trip traces are.

debug.symptom: Riders wait too long for a match
steps: Check supply and demand for that city: it may simply be too few drivers.
Open a slow match trace: nearby search, the maps ETA call, or the lock?
Check the maps provider latency and error rate.
Check geo index shard load for that city.
Check gateway connections per node: a node near its limit drops connections.
Check recent gateway deploys: draining connections too fast causes reconnect storms.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Geo routed: sends each app to the region that serves its area (Route 53 geolocation resolves to a country or US state, so a finer city split needs a regional hostname chosen by the app)

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Web ACL on the load balancer: managed rules, rate rules per IP, bot control; inspects WebSocket upgrades, not frames

nodes.label: Load Balancer (L7)
nodes.description: Terminates TLS; keeps each WebSocket pinned to one gateway

nodes.label: WebSocket Gateway
nodes.description: Holds one persistent connection per online driver and rider; records which instance holds each user in a connection registry

nodes.label: Matching Service
nodes.description: Finds and locks the best nearby driver

nodes.label: Driver Geo Index
nodes.description: Redis, sharded by city: available drivers (GEO set), heartbeats, offer leases and busy flags, and the connection registry

nodes.label: Trips DB
nodes.description: Trips, status, fares, GPS traces; at most one active trip per driver (partial unique index)

nodes.label: Location Stream
nodes.description: Every location ping, partitioned by driver id; read by the Trip Tracker here, and by ETA-model and analytics pipelines outside this design

nodes.label: Trip Tracker
nodes.description: Reads the location stream: pushes on-trip drivers' positions to their rider and appends each trip's GPS trace

flows.title: Driver location update
flows.summary: Every ~4 s each online driver sends a position. This is the highest-volume path in the system.

steps.label: WS frame: location
steps.detail: Sent over an already-open WebSocket: no new connection or TLS handshake per update. The WAF inspected the upgrade request when the connection opened (a valid token, rate rules per IP); frames on an open connection pass straight through.

steps.label: pinned gateway
steps.detail: The load balancer keeps each WebSocket pinned to the gateway instance that accepted it.

steps.label: update(d_7781, lat, lng)
steps.detail: Location Service instances are stateless, so the gateway hands each update to any of them over a pooled internal connection.

steps.label: update position (script)
steps.detail: Only the latest position matters, so this is an in-memory overwrite: ~250k writes/s fits a Redis cluster sharded by city, where a disk-based database would struggle. One script keeps busy drivers out of the available set and refreshes a 30 s heartbeat, so a driver whose app goes silent drops out of matching.
steps.payload:
EVALSHA update_pos 3 drivers:{sf}:available busy:{sf}:d_7781 hb:{sf}:d_7781 -122.4192 37.7793 d_7781
-- if busy:{sf}:d_7781 exists: ZREM it from the available set, return its trip id
-- else GEOADD drivers:{sf}:available -122.4192 37.7793 d_7781
-- always SET hb:{sf}:d_7781 1 EX 30

steps.label: append location event
steps.detail: The full history goes to a stream, partitioned by driver id and tagged with the trip id when the driver is busy. The geo index stays small and hot.

steps.label: d_4410 on t_548
steps.detail: Only updates from drivers on a trip matter here; the tracker skips the rest. Take a driver d_4410 who is driving rider r_19 on trip t_548.

steps.label: append trace batch
steps.detail: Points are buffered per trip and written about every 30 s as one row, which keeps the database load to tens of thousands of small writes a second instead of 125k. The trace is what the fare is computed from.

steps.label: push position to r_19
steps.detail: Any gateway instance can take the push.

steps.label: which gateway holds r_19?
steps.detail: Each gateway records its connections in the registry when a client connects, so a reconnect to another instance updates it at once.

steps.label: frame on r_19's connection
steps.detail: Forwarded to instance ws-17, which writes the frame on the rider's open WebSocket.

flows.title: Request a ride
flows.summary: Find nearby drivers, rank by real road ETA, lock one so nobody else can take it, and offer the trip.

steps.label: resolve api.rides.example.com
steps.detail: Geo routing (by country or US state in Route 53) or a regional hostname chosen by the app sends each app to its city's region, so the rider, the driver and the matching service for that city share a region. A short TTL lets traffic move if a region fails.

steps.label: POST /trips
steps.payload:
POST /trips HTTP/2
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci…
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c…

{ "quote_id": "q_88", "pickup": [37.7793, -122.4192], "dropoff": [37.8080, -122.4177], "product": "standard" }
steps.detail: The quote the rider accepted fixes the price and surge multiplier they were shown.

steps.label: managed rules + rate rules
steps.detail: The web ACL blocks exploit patterns, caps requests per IP and challenges scripted clients, which is where fake-account and promo-abuse traffic comes from.

steps.label: route
steps.detail: The load balancer health-checks the Trip Service instances across three zones and starts the trace; the trace id goes with every hop to matching and the maps call.

steps.label: INSERT trip REQUESTED
steps.detail: The idempotency key makes a retried tap return the same trip instead of creating two. The trip stores the quote's price and surge.

steps.label: match(t_552)
steps.detail: The rider's POST waits like a long poll, capped at about 30 s. If no driver has accepted by then, it returns 202 and the result reaches the rider app over its WebSocket.

steps.label: GEOSEARCH 2 km
steps.payload: GEOSEARCH drivers:{sf}:available FROMLONLAT -122.4192 37.7793 BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 10
steps.detail: Candidates whose heartbeat key has expired are skipped (and a sweep removes them from the set), so drivers whose app died are not offered trips.

steps.label: 10 nearest drivers
steps.detail: Straight-line nearest, which is only a first cut.

steps.label: ETA matrix 10×1
steps.detail: Rivers, bridges and one-way streets make straight-line distance misleading, so candidates are ranked by road ETA.

steps.label: SET busy:d_7781 t_552 NX EX 15
steps.detail: Atomic claim: two matchers serving two riders can never offer the same driver at once. The 15 s expiry frees the driver if they ignore the offer, and the next location update puts them back in the available set.

steps.label: push offer to d_7781
steps.detail: Any gateway instance accepts the push and looks up which instance holds the driver's connection.

steps.label: which gateway holds d_7781?
steps.detail: The connection registry maps each online user to the gateway instance holding their socket.

steps.label: WS push: offer
steps.detail: Instance ws-4 writes the offer on the driver's open WebSocket.

steps.label: accepted(t_552)
steps.detail: The accept carries the trip id, so a late accept for an older offer is ignored.

steps.label: keep d_7781 busy if still t_552
steps.detail: The lease may have expired while the driver was deciding. A small script makes the busy flag permanent only if it still names this trip, and takes the driver out of the available set.
steps.payload:
EVALSHA confirm_busy 2 busy:{sf}:d_7781 drivers:{sf}:available t_552 d_7781
-- if GET busy == t_552: PERSIST busy, ZREM available d_7781, return 1
-- else return 0 (lease lost: offer the next candidate)

steps.label: UPDATE … WHERE status='REQUESTED'
steps.detail: Conditional update: if the rider cancelled meanwhile, zero rows change and the driver is released. A partial unique index allows one active trip per driver, so even if a Redis failover lost the busy flag, the database refuses a second assignment.

steps.label: driver arriving in 3 min
steps.detail: From here, the rider app follows the driver's position over its own WebSocket (see the location flow).

flows.title: Complete trip and pay
flows.summary: Compute the fare from the actual route, then charge exactly once.

steps.label: route distance + duration
steps.detail: Uses the trip's GPS trace, which the Trip Tracker appended to the trip as it went, snapped to roads.

steps.label: fare = base + km + min × surge
steps.detail: The surge multiplier comes from the quote the rider accepted before requesting, stored on the trip, so the rider pays the price they were shown. Pricing itself runs outside this design.

steps.label: charge, key = t_552
steps.detail: The trip id is the idempotency key: if the call times out and is retried, the provider returns the first result instead of charging twice. The call leaves through the NAT gateway.

steps.label: UPDATE COMPLETED, fare
steps.detail: If the provider is down, the trip is still marked COMPLETED with payment pending, and a background job in the Trip Service retries the charge with the same key (Stripe keeps keys for at least 24 hours, so a retry after that first looks the charge up by trip id).

steps.label: release d_7781 from t_552
steps.detail: The driver is free again only once the trip is finished in the database.

steps.label: DEL busy if still t_552
steps.detail: Compare and delete, so a stale release can never free a driver who has since started another trip.
steps.payload:
EVALSHA release_busy 1 busy:{sf}:d_7781 t_552
-- if GET busy == t_552: DEL busy

steps.label: trip complete
steps.detail: The driver goes back into the available set on their next location update, now that the busy flag is gone.

notes.text: Shard by city (or by H3 / geohash prefix). A rider's search only touches one shard, and hot cities get more shards.

Redis replicates asynchronously. After a failover, positions refill within seconds from the next pings, but recent busy flags may be lost, so a driver on a trip could reappear as available. The partial unique index on active trips per driver in the Trips DB refuses the second assignment, and matching moves on to the next candidate.
WebSockets push offers instantly and avoid 1M clients polling. Cost: stateful connections, so gateways need connection draining on deploys and clients must auto-reconnect.
Nearest driver is not always best. Production systems batch requests for a second or two and solve a small assignment problem to lower total pickup time.
Payment provider down: mark the trip COMPLETED with payment pending and retry from a background job. Never block the driver's next trip on payment.

ALB vs NLB: an application (L7) load balancer handles WebSockets and adds TLS termination and path routing. At ~1M long-lived driver connections, many teams put a network (L4) load balancer in front of the WebSocket gateways instead: higher connection limits, lower latency, static IPs, and the gateways terminate TLS themselves.

Geo routing keeps a city in one region, which keeps the driver geo index and matching local. Other regions run copies of this design. If a region fails, change the DNS answer and drivers reconnect to another region within a few minutes (about one TTL); trips in progress continue only if the Trips DB is replicated there.

The web ACL on the load balancer inspects every HTTP request and each WebSocket upgrade (frames on an open connection are not inspected): managed rule sets, per-IP rate rules and bot control against fake accounts and scripted ride requests. Both apps send short-lived tokens checked by the gateway on connect and by the Trip Service on every call; the payment provider key lives in the secrets manager.

questions.q: Drivers send their location every few seconds. How do you handle that write volume?
questions.a: Treat locations as ephemeral: keep only the latest position per driver in an in-memory geo index, not a database row per update. Drivers stream over persistent WebSocket connections so there is no per-update handshake. The full history goes to a stream for analytics, off the hot path.

questions.q: How do you find nearby available drivers quickly?
questions.a: Index drivers by a geospatial cell such as a geohash or H3 cell, then look up the rider's cell and its neighbours. That turns a search over every driver into a few small lookups. Cell size is a trade-off: too large returns many candidates to filter, too small needs many neighbouring cells.

questions.q: Two riders are offered the same driver at the same moment. How do you prevent a double booking?
questions.a: Make the claim atomic: matching sets a busy flag for the driver only if none exists (SET NX with a short expiry), so only one request wins and the other moves to the next candidate. On accept, the flag is kept only if it still names this trip. The driver is written onto the trip with a conditional update, and a partial unique index allowing one active trip per driver is the final guard if Redis ever loses a flag.

questions.q: A WebSocket gateway instance dies. What happens to the connected drivers and riders?
questions.a: Their connections drop and the apps reconnect, with backoff and jitter, through the load balancer to another instance. Nothing important lived only in the gateway: trip state is in the Trips DB and positions are refreshed by the next update. On reconnect the new instance overwrites the user's entry in the connection registry, so pushes find it at once.

questions.q: The payment provider times out at the end of a trip. Was the rider charged?
questions.a: You do not know, so never blindly retry a charge. Send every charge with an idempotency key tied to the trip, so a retry returns the original result instead of charging twice. Mark the trip as payment pending and reconcile with the provider asynchronously; the rider can leave immediately.

questions.q: How would you compute surge pricing?
questions.a: Aggregate supply (available drivers) and demand (ride requests) per geo cell over a short sliding window from the location stream and request counts, in a pricing job outside this design. Price is a function of the ratio, smoothed so it does not flicker. The multiplier is locked into the quote the rider accepts, stored on the trip, and used for the fare.
